title: Build a Min-Heap
prompt:
JavaScript has no built-in priority queue, so build the one you'll reuse. A min-heap stores items in an array laid out as a tree (children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2; the parent is at Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)). The smallest item is always at index 0.

API:

  • new MinHeap(compare): compare(a, b) returns a negative number when a should come out first. Default (a, b) => a - b.
  • push(value): add, then bubble up while smaller than the parent. O(log n).
  • pop(): remove and return the smallest (undefined if empty). Move the last item to the top, then sink down while larger than the smaller child. O(log n).
  • peek(): the smallest without removing it (undefined if empty). O(1).
  • size(): number of items.

Example: push 5, 1, 3; pop returns 1, then 3, then 5.

tests.name: pops in ascending order
peek shows the smallest without removing it
empty heap
sorts a scrambled array (heap sort) with duplicates and negatives
interleaved pushes and pops
custom comparator: max-heap
custom comparator: [priority, name] pairs
keeps the array a valid heap (no full re-sort)

hints: The heap rule is only "every parent is <= its children". Siblings can be in any order. After a push or pop, only one path from top to bottom can be broken, so you only fix that path: O(log n).

push: start at the last index; while it has a parent and compare(item, parent) < 0, swap them and move up. pop: save items[0]; pop the last item; if anything is left, put it at index 0 and sink: swap with the smaller child while that child is smaller.

Sink-down shape:

while (true) {
  const left = 2 * index + 1, right = 2 * index + 2;
  let smallest = index;
  if (left < n && this.compare(this.items[left], this.items[smallest]) < 0) smallest = left;
  if (right < n && this.compare(this.items[right], this.items[smallest]) < 0) smallest = right;
  if (smallest === index) break;
  [this.items[index], this.items[smallest]] = [this.items[smallest], this.items[index]];
  index = smallest;
}
explain:
push and pop are O(log n) because a heap of n items is a complete tree about log₂ n levels tall, and each operation walks one path. peek is O(1). Space O(n). You now own the class the next two labs (and Dijkstra, schedulers and "merge k sorted lists") build on.

Say it: "JavaScript has no heap, so I'll use a small array-backed binary heap: push bubbles up, pop moves the last item to the root and sinks it. Both O(log n)." In an interview it's usually fine to say "assume a MinHeap class with push, pop, peek" and write it only if asked.
